articleTitle: Some facts concerning the life and character of rontgen
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Wilhelm Conrad Böntgen was born in 1845. At the ago of 25 years he published his first scientific work, when 50 he made his great discovery, and at 78 he left us. Those who made the acquaintance of the youthful Röntgen would hardly have prophesied for him the career of a famous scientist. No doubt his embracing love of Nature, his urge to get at the root of things, and his tendency towards experiment made themselves evident even in his childhood. He appears to have been rather a poor than a good scholar. An event not accurately known — perhaps a default on the part of one of his fellow-pupils, in which Röntgen was innocently involved, compelled him to break off his studies without having obtained his school-leaving certificate.

articleTitle: The starting characteristics of induction type motors
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The three-phase induction motor finds a wide field of application in most modern industries owing to its low initial cost, comparative ease of starting and low cost of starting equipment. A further advantage is its low cost of maintenance. It has, however, the disadvantage of poor power factor when running on reduced loads. The synchronous motor, on the other hand, has the characteristic of good power factor, together with the possibility of power factor improvement, but it suffers from the disadvantage that it will not run up from rest. For this reason, various types of synchronous motors and machines, such as synchronous condensers and rotary condensers and rotary converters, which may be run up either by a separate induction motor or by a separate induction winding built into the machine itself, have been evolved.

articleTitle: “Some notes on british switch-gear practice”
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: Prior to the last six years, new types of circuit-breakers and improvements in detail were based to a considerable extent on service experiences and tests on supply systems. Progress, always rapid, has now been accelerated by routine testing at short-circuit testing stations, and recent developments in the art of circuit-breaking have been far reaching. Although a number of new types of circuit-breakers have been produced, the object of British manufacturers has, on the whole, been rather to improve existing designs than to introduce completely new generic kinds of switchgear. On the continent of Europe the tendency has been along the lines of eliminating oil from circuit-breakers, whereas in Great Britain and the united States of America the reliability of the oil circuit-breaker has been established and has been the basis of recent developments.

articleTitle: “THe lightning discharge”
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The last occasion on which I was privileged to lecture in this manner before the Institute was lour years ago, in July, 1933. Our lightning research programme was then just beginning and I was able to show on the screen the first and very promising results which had been obtained from it. In the intervening four years, as you will have learnt from the Annual Reports of the Council, a great deal of bard work has been done and a great deal of information has been obtained. As you know, the main problem which the Lightning Research Committee set itself to attack was the actual nature of the lightning discharge. In all questions of lightning protection of transmission and distribution lines (here I quote from a recent report by Mr. K. B. McEachron of the General Electrical Company), “the greatest unknown was the lightning stroke itself. ... It was evident that a more thorough knowledge of the lightning stroke would lead to a better undemanding of its effects on lines and apparatus, and would provide a more substantial basis for design and for testing technique.” This, then, was our object and if one can judge from the widespread interest taken in our results, we have been successful both in the problem we chose to tackle and in the solution we have reached. For this we have to thank the various members of our Committees who helped to make it a success, those who organised the investigations and watched over their financial support, those who actually operated the instruments which we designed and constructed, and those who studied the records to interpret their meaning.

articleTitle: Switching transients on overhead transmission lines and the effect of a cable upon them
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The subject of electrical transients is a very important one, embracing as it does a study of the conditions prevailing whenever the steady amount of stored energy la a circuit is changed. Therefore any operation such as switching, lightning disturbances, etc., which produce a change in the circuit conditions, resulting in a decrease or increase in the amount of stored energy will produce a transient. The energy may be present in one or more different form's and the resulting transient is known as a single-energy or dougle-energy transient respectively. The two common types of energy storage when dealing with electrical phenomena are the dielectric and magnetic fields, as exemplified by the simple condenser and choke coil.

articleTitle: “The lightning discharge”
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: In his very interesting paper, Professor Schonland has shown that the theoretical protection offered by a lighning conductor does not correspond with observed results: he put forward the belief that the horizontal zone protected at ground level has a radius equal to the vertical height of the conductor. This, however does not seem to be a hard and fast rule, for I have known a lightning stroke to hit the ground quite near the base of a two-storey house which was thought to be protected by a lightning conductor fixed on to the chimney stack. A worthy explanation of this apparent uselessness of a lightning conductor may be found in F. J. Miranda's discussion of Professor B. L. Goodlet's paper on “Lightning,” in the July, 1937, issue of the I.E.E. Journal. It is there shown experiment ally that, under certain voltage conditions, a lightning discharge may not always take the shortest path to earth. It would seem, therefore, that as the conditions of generation of a lightning discharge are beyond human control it is quite useless constructing a vertical lightning conductor in the hope that it will be reliable.

articleTitle: An investigation of methods of measuring the resistance of earth connections
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: During the past few years, a number of papers have been delivered by Students before this Institution on the subject of earth resistance and the earthing of systems. Their main object has been the investigation of phenomena and problems connected with the earthing of systems, and much valuable data has been collected. The subject has by no means been exhausted, however, and the authors of this paper decided to compare the methods employed for making earthing resistance measurements, It was felt that information on this aspect of the subject might prove of some practical value. The object of this paper, therefore, is to correlate various methods of measuring earthing resistances, and to investigate their relative accuracy.

articleTitle: AN investigation into the behaviour of selenium contact rectifiers
publicationTitle: Transactions of the South African Institute of Electrical Engineers
abstract: The earliest report on contact rectification dates back to 1874 when Braun published the results he obtained from experiments with natural metallic sulphides and also with some specially prepared compounds suitably arranged between contact clamps. Branley subsequently studied the rectifying properties of copper oxide in contact with different metals. In 1904, Midgley described a detector consisting of an asymmetrical junction between a metal such as silver and a metal oxide such as silver oxide or copper oxide. In the following four years the crystal detector appeared and reports on the characteristics of crystal detectors or rectifiers were published by Dunwoody, Pearce and others. In 1908 Thompson patented the first copper oxide rectifier. This consisted of a small copper disc on the one edge of which an artificial layer of oxide was produced by the action of heat. This was pressed against a soft metal electrode of lead or tin. In the years following up to 1925 may types of contact rectifiers were described and patented The latter year saw the commercial development the contact rectifiers. The two principal developments were the cupric sulphide rectifier described by Ruben, and the copper oxide rectifier described by Grondahl and his associates. The former type is of the low resistance class and is mainly used for high current densities. This type has received scant treatment in the literature on the subject. The latter type is of the high resistance class and is better adapted to the case where the current to be passed is small.

abstract: The Council is empowered each year at its discretion to award the Gold Medal of the Institute, together with a certificate and, if considered desirable, a premium not exceeding £10 10s., to a member of any grade for an original paper of outstanding merit submitted during the year. It is also authorised to award at its discretion the Bronze Medal of the Institute, together with a certificate and, if considered desirable, a premium not exceeding £5 5s., to a member of the Student grade for an original paper of outstanding merit submitted by a member of that grade.
